items.title: Market Watch: Britain's Forgotten Cars Are Making a Comeback
items.summary: As The New Yardstick reaches its 75th article and launches its Instagram account, we're taking a moment to look beyond new vehicle launches and future technologies. While exploring Instagram's automotive community, we discovered a surprisingly enthusiastic following for the ordinary cars of the 1990s and 2000s. From dedicated owners to small enthusiast…
items.content_html:
As The New Yardstick reaches its 75th article and launches its Instagram account, we're taking a moment to look beyond new vehicle launches and future technologies.

While exploring Instagram's automotive community, we discovered a surprisingly enthusiastic following for the ordinary cars of the 1990s and 2000s. From dedicated owners to small enthusiast pages, there's considerable affection for models that were once an everyday sight on British roads.

And this enthusiasm extends well beyond social media. Hagerty's 2026 Festival of the Unexceptional attracted around 2,500 cars and more than 4,500 visitors, celebrating the everyday vehicles that rarely received much attention when new.

Many of these cars are gradually disappearing, yet their appeal seems to be growing. Some are becoming modern classics, while others remain remarkably affordable.


Once a familiar sight on British roads, the Citroën ZX has become one of the more overlooked family hatchbacks of the 1990s.

Our search uncovered a 1994 1.9D Avantage advertised for £1,995, with 122,000 miles, full service history and the same keeper for 20 years. Its sunroof and reportedly original towbar add period charm, although towing with just 71bhp must require some patience.

The naturally aspirated 1.9-litre diesel offers straightforward engineering and excellent economy, while the ZX's clever rear suspension made it surprisingly enjoyable to drive. Corrosion, rear-axle wear and timing-belt maintenance deserve attention.

Another 1.9D, a 1992 example showing 89,000 miles and some cosmetic wear, is advertised for £1,850. With so few available, we'd suggest a provisional £1,500–£2,500 shopping budget rather than a firm market average.

Turbo-diesel versions occasionally appear too, although the recent British adverts we located have since been removed.


The Ford Fusion arrived in 2002 with a straightforward idea: take the critically acclaimed Fiesta and give it a taller body, easier access and more luggage space. It offered many of the same mechanical strengths, but at a higher price and without quite the same charm.

Critics found its styling uninspiring and its ride surprisingly firm, while sales never approached those of its hatchback sibling. Ford subsequently introduced the B-Max, followed by the EcoSport, before the Puma finally made the raised, practical small Ford a mainstream favourite.

Today, the Fusion's lack of status is part of its appeal. We've found a 1.4 advertised for just £995 and a 1.6 automatic for £1,995, both with fewer than 80,000 miles.

Neither is a collectible rarity, but both offer inexpensive, practical transport. Buyers should check for corrosion, suspension wear and evidence of regular maintenance.

The Fusion may never become a celebrated classic, but does it deserve more recognition for anticipating the small crossover trend?


The Hyundai Matrix has always divided opinion, but time has arguably been kinder to its styling than expected. Its straight-edged profile, distinctive stepped window line and generous glass areas look surprisingly considered today, particularly knowing it was designed by Pininfarina.

Hyundai's transformation into a respected global manufacturer also makes its earlier, more unconventional models interesting to revisit.

Launched in 2001, the Matrix prioritised everyday practicality, offering a spacious interior, elevated seating position and generous accommodation within compact dimensions. Its straightforward 1.6-litre petrol engine remains a sensible choice, although buyers should inspect the underside for corrosion and check suspension wear.

Our search uncovered a 2006 1.6 manual for £995, a 2008 example with 84,000 miles for £1,250, and another 2007 manual for £1,450. Automatics are also plentiful, with examples advertised between approximately £1,000 and £2,200.

A future classic? Perhaps not conventionally, but the Matrix is an increasingly interesting reminder of Hyundai's earlier design ambitions.


Unlike many cars in this collection, the MG F was a genuine success when new. Launched in 1995, it became Britain's bestselling sports car for six consecutive years, with more than 40,000 UK sales. Yet today, the Mazda MX-5 arguably receives much greater recognition, while the MG F remains surprisingly affordable.

With its mid-mounted 1.8-litre engine, rear-wheel drive and distinctive Hydragas suspension, the MG offered an engaging alternative to conventional front-engined roadsters.

Our search uncovered a 1998 example with just 45,500 miles for £1,995, including recent cambelt and water-pump replacement. Other ordinary examples are advertised from approximately £1,100–£2,200. Buyers should investigate head-gasket history, suspension condition and corrosion.

The MG F also represents a very different chapter in MG's history. Today's brand concentrates on modern family cars, SUVs and electrification, although the all-electric Cyberster has finally revived its roadster tradition.

Perhaps it's time this once-popular British sports car received renewed appreciation.


The Mitsubishi Space Star was never a car to set pulses racing, but perhaps that's precisely why it deserves another look.

Sitting somewhere between a conventional hatchback and a small MPV, it offered generous interior space, comfortable seating and straightforward mechanicals, yet remained largely overlooked alongside more fashionable rivals.

Our search uncovered a particularly tidy 1.6-litre petrol example for £1,500. With just 54,000 miles, full service history, a year's MOT, sunroof, alloy wheels and air conditioning, it offers a surprising amount of everyday car for the money. The manual 1.6 was also capable of nearly 40mpg on the official combined cycle.

Elsewhere, we found a 1.6 automatic advertised for £999 and a manual for £1,740, suggesting a typical asking-price range of approximately £1,000–£2,000.

With Mitsubishi's reputation for durability, the Space Star represents affordable, practical motoring. It might never become a valuable classic, but perhaps it deserves recognition simply for being an honest, dependable family car.


The final Nissan Primera was an unconventional family car. Introduced in 2002, its unusual styling and centrally mounted instruments divided opinion, while the Toyota Avensis, Ford Mondeo and Vauxhall Vectra remained more familiar choices.

Available as a hatchback, saloon and estate, it also reminds us how much the market has changed. Nissan no longer offers a conventional saloon or estate in Britain, with its larger family models now dominated by SUVs and crossovers.

Beneath that distinctive exterior sat a spacious, comfortable and generally dependable car. Equipment was generous, with climate control standard and reversing cameras on many versions. The 1.8-litre petrol is a sensible choice, although buyers should check for oil consumption, timing-chain noises and electrical faults.

Our search uncovered a 2006 Primera 1.8 Flare manual with 70,841 miles for £995, while a 1.8 SE automatic was advertised for £1,499. Other examples suggest a realistic asking-price range of approximately £1,000–£2,000, excluding recorded insurance write-offs.

As affordable family transport, the overlooked P12 still makes considerable sense.


Launched in 2002, the Peugeot 307 SW offered something unusual: the practicality of a family estate with the option of seven seats. Competitively priced when new, with substantial dealer discounts adding to its appeal, it provided an affordable alternative to larger people carriers.

Its generous interior, panoramic glass roof and individually removable rear seats made it surprisingly versatile, although not every example included the optional sixth and seventh seats.

Buyers could choose from several petrol and HDi diesel engines. Today, the straightforward 1.6-litre petrol is arguably a safer choice than some later, more complex diesels, although the early 90bhp 2.0 HDi remains appealing. Electrical problems and general maintenance history deserve particular attention.

Our search uncovered 1.6 petrol examples around £995 and 2.0 HDi diesels from approximately £1,195. We also found seven-seat examples advertised for £850 and £1,850.

Overlooked and frequently dismissed, the 307 SW remains a remarkably practical family car for very little money.


Once an everyday sight on British roads, the original Renault Mégane is becoming increasingly difficult to find. Introduced in 1996, it replaced the Renault 19 and developed into a surprisingly extensive family, including a five-door hatchback, Classic saloon, Coupé, Cabriolet and the pioneering Scénic MPV.

An estate was also offered in mainland Europe, while the rugged four-wheel-drive Scénic RX4 later joined the extended family.

Today, it's the ordinary hatchback that feels particularly interesting. Its rounded styling has aged gracefully, while the 1.6-litre petrol remains a sensible choice. Cambelt history, cooling systems and ageing electrics deserve attention.

Our search uncovered a 1998 Mégane 1.6 RXE for £1,795, with just 42,000 miles and one owner from new. Garaged for 12 years, it has recently received a new cambelt, water pump, tyres and fluids. Another 2000 1.6 manual was advertised for £1,500.

Once commonplace, these cars are now becoming unusual simply because so few survive. Perhaps the unremarkable Mégane is finally becoming interesting.


The eighth-generation Toyota Corolla arrived in 1997 with unusually distinctive styling. Its rounded headlights earned it the nickname 'bug-eye', although buyers remained more interested in Toyota's reputation for reliability than its newfound character.

Available as a hatchback, liftback, saloon and estate, the Corolla offered comfortable, dependable family transport. The modest 1.3-litre petrol was never particularly quick, but its simplicity and durability were considerable strengths.

There's personal experience behind this choice. A T-registration 1.3 Corolla passed through three generations of our editor's family, proving itself comfortable, reliable and thoroughly unremarkable in the best possible way.

Our search uncovered a 1998 1.3 with just 37,476 miles for £1,200, alongside a 1999 example showing 53,000 miles for £1,295. Buyers should pay attention to corrosion, cambelt history and ageing suspension components.

While sporting Corollas attract increasing interest, these ordinary versions remain largely forgotten. Perhaps it's time the dependable everyday Corolla received some recognition.


Introduced in 2003, the Vauxhall Signum was an unusual attempt to turn the familiar Vectra into something approaching an executive car. With an extended wheelbase, generous rear legroom and sliding, reclining rear seats, it offered considerable comfort without the expense of a traditional luxury saloon.

An optional Travel Assistant even provided folding tables and a small fridge. Unfortunately, buyers struggled to understand where the Signum fitted into Vauxhall's range, and sales never really took off.

Our search uncovered a 2006 Signum 1.9 CDTi manual with 73,000 miles for £1,300, complete with a recently replaced clutch and flywheel. Another 2006 diesel automatic was advertised for £1,499, while a 2.2-litre petrol automatic appeared for £1,900.

Buyers should check diesel cambelt and water-pump history, inlet swirl flaps on the 150bhp CDTi, timing-chain condition on 2.2-litre petrol models and ageing electronics. The Signum never found its audience when new, but its unusual combination of space, comfort and affordability looks increasingly appealing today.

– These ten cars may never become highly valuable classics, but perhaps that's part of their appeal. They remind us of a time when ordinary family cars came in all shapes and sizes, often offering character, practicality and dependability without attracting much attention.

What began as an exploration of Instagram's automotive community has revealed something rather encouraging: these forgotten cars still have enthusiastic owners and admirers.

With a budget of £2,500, there are still opportunities to enjoy a little overlooked motoring history. Whether it's a dependable Corolla, an unusual Signum or a once-popular MG F, perhaps a car doesn't need to be particularly special to deserve being remembered.

Prices quoted are advertised UK asking prices identified during October 2026 and may change as vehicles are sold or listings are removed. Vehicle specifications, mileage, condition and history are based on advertised information and have not been independently verified. Buyers should undertake their own checks before purchasing.

items.title: A New Luxury Empire – Inside BYD's Plans to Challenge the Establishment
items.summary: For most British buyers, BYD remains a relatively new name, associated primarily with affordable electric cars and increasingly competitive family SUVs. Yet behind those familiar models sits a much more ambitious operation, one now reaching into territory traditionally occupied by Rolls-Royce. The latest indication is the Yangwang Altior, an imposing new luxury…
items.content_html:
Our interpretation of the Yangwang Altior draws on the limited previews released so far, with an imposing vertical grille, substantial bonnet, rear-hinged doors and unmistakably formal proportions. Although expected to measure approximately 5.5 metres long, almost matching the Rolls-Royce Ghost, its commanding appearance feels closer to the larger Phantom.

Chinese reports suggest a wheelbase of around 3,350mm, promising generous accommodation for rear passengers. Mechanical specifications remain unconfirmed, although Yangwang's existing e⁴ architecture raises the possibility of four independently driven electric motors, potentially accompanied by sophisticated active suspension.

For comparison, the Rolls-Royce Ghost starts at approximately £290,000 in Britain, powered by a 6.75-litre twin-turbocharged V12 producing 571PS. The Yangwang Altior is expected to make its world debut in the UAE in early November, giving BYD its clearest opportunity yet to demonstrate how its vision of ultra-luxury motoring differs from Europe's established marques.

From what we've seen so far, BYD certainly isn't lacking ambition. Whether it can match Rolls-Royce's exceptional refinement and craftsmanship remains another question.


BYD's premium ambitions are already taking shape in Britain. Denza, founded in 2010 as a partnership between BYD and Daimler, now occupies the group's premium tier, while Yangwang sits above it as its ultra-luxury marque.

The Z9 GT is leading Denza's British introduction. This striking electric shooting brake enters the same territory as the Polestar 5 and Lotus Emeya, two other Chinese-built grand tourers with established European identities. At £105,000 for the fully electric model, Denza has chosen to compete confidently rather than simply undercut its rivals. A £95,000 plug-in hybrid will follow.

Its headline figures are substantial: three electric motors producing 1,156PS, a 122kWh battery and up to 373 miles of WLTP range. At a compatible FLASH charger, replenishing the battery from 10–70% takes just five minutes.

Perhaps most intriguing is its independently controlled rear-wheel steering, allowing the car to move diagonally, perform a complete 360-degree compass turn and achieve a turning radius of just 5.35 metres.

For a relatively unfamiliar name entering Britain's premium market, that's quite an introduction.


Where the Z9 GT sets out to thrill its driver, the Denza D9 is considerably more concerned with its passengers. This substantial seven-seat luxury MPV takes aim directly at the Lexus LM, combining generous accommodation, powered sliding doors and an interior designed to resemble a first-class lounge.

Denza has confirmed British prices of £75,000 for the Elegance and £85,000 for the Ultimate, comfortably undercutting the Lexus LM, which starts at £97,645.

The flagship D9 features individual second-row entertainment screens and zero-gravity seats with 16-point massage functions, capable of reclining to 152 degrees. The emphasis is firmly on relaxation rather than performance.

Underneath, an all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid system combines a 1.5-litre petrol engine with two electric motors and a substantial 58.5kWh battery. Denza claims up to 130 miles of electric-only range and 590 miles combined, while compatible FLASH chargers can add approximately 80 miles of electric driving range in just five minutes.

It's a very different expression of premium motoring from the Z9 GT, demonstrating just how broad Denza's ambitions have become.


From first-class transport to open-top grand touring, Denza's next offering is considerably more theatrical. The Z is a four-seat electric grand tourer offered in Coupé, Spider and more aggressive Racing versions. Its proportions and character suggest competition with the Maserati GranCabrio and Ferrari's new Amalfi Spider.

Denza has already announced British prices: £142,900 for the Coupé, £159,900 for the Spider and £172,900 for the Racing.

All three feature a 76kWh battery and three electric motors producing 1,604PS. Even the open-top Spider reaches 62mph in just 2.3 seconds, while the Racing version can achieve 1.96 seconds with optional semi-slick tyres.

Carbon-ceramic brakes, sophisticated suspension and a four-seat interior demonstrate the intention to combine serious performance with grand touring comfort, while retaining compatibility with BYD's FLASH Charging technology.

For Denza, it's another ambitious step into territory traditionally dominated by established European marques.

Above Denza sits Yangwang, BYD's ultra-luxury division, and the U8 demonstrates its unconventional approach to the Range Rover's territory.

Measuring 5.32 metres long, the U8 combines four independently controlled electric motors producing almost 1,200PS with a petrol range extender. Despite weighing over three tonnes, it reaches 62mph in approximately 3.5 seconds.

Independent wheel control enables a 360-degree tank turn, while emergency flotation allows the vehicle to remain temporarily afloat in deep water. Inside, Nappa leather, advanced suspension and extensive digital displays provide the expected luxury.

The longer U8L adds more rear-passenger space, including an exclusive four-seat configuration. Chinese prices start at approximately £113,000 for the U8 and £146,000 for the U8L. Allowing for UK costs, TNY estimates potential prices of £150,000–£175,000 and £190,000–£225,000 respectively.

The U8L appeared at Goodwood in 2026, with Yangwang planning a British introduction in 2027, although official prices remain unconfirmed.


At the top of Yangwang's performance range sits the U9, an electric supercar designed to demonstrate what BYD's engineering can achieve.

Its four electric motors produce approximately 1,300hp, delivering 0–62mph in just 2.36 seconds. The advanced DiSus-X suspension can even make the car jump or perform a controlled dance, something demonstrated at Goodwood in July.

The U9 Xtreme takes things considerably further. Producing over 3,000PS from four motors, it reached 308.3mph in September 2025, setting a production-car speed record. It also completed the Nürburgring Nordschleife in just 6 minutes 59.157 seconds. Production is limited to 30 examples, with European availability confirmed.

The U9 is Yangwang's halo car, demonstrating the technology and engineering capabilities behind the badge.

Alongside the U8's versatility and Denza's expanding luxury range, these achievements give the forthcoming Altior considerable promise. BYD has already demonstrated its engineering ability; the next challenge is matching the craftsmanship, comfort and refinement expected at the very top of the luxury market.


The Yangwang Altior could become the clearest expression yet of BYD's ambitions at the very top of the automotive market. Our final rendering imagines a substantial, elegantly proportioned luxury saloon, although the production car's appearance and specifications remain to be confirmed.

What makes the project particularly interesting is the strength of the wider group behind it. Denza is already preparing to compete with established premium manufacturers in Britain, while Yangwang has demonstrated engineering capabilities that extend from sophisticated luxury SUVs to record-breaking electric hypercars.

Yet competing with Rolls-Royce presents a different challenge. Beyond performance and technology, buyers expect exceptional craftsmanship, refinement, personalisation and an ownership experience developed over generations.

BYD has the financial resources, engineering expertise and growing international presence to make a serious attempt. Whether it can establish the same desirability and prestige as Europe's most established luxury manufacturers remains to be seen.

The question is no longer whether BYD can build expensive cars, but whether it can create a luxury brand that customers genuinely aspire to own.

items.title: Two Forgotten Names, One Electric Future – Reimagining the Nissan Figaro and Renault Wind
items.summary: Small electric cars are finally becoming affordable, but that doesn't mean they all need to follow the same formula. Renault's new Twingo E-Tech demonstrates what can be achieved with compact, cost-effective electric engineering, raising an intriguing question about what else those foundations could support. For TNY Design Studio, two names immediately spring to…
items.content_html:
The new Renault Twingo E-Tech electric represents an important step towards making small electric cars genuinely affordable.

Measuring just 3.79 metres long, it combines a 27.5kWh LFP battery with an 82hp electric motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range. Its five-door body, sliding rear seats and surprisingly versatile interior demonstrate just how much practicality can be squeezed into a genuinely compact car.

Yet the Twingo's greatest potential may extend beyond Renault's own showrooms. Its adapted AmpR Small architecture provides a modern electric foundation that could be shared across several models, reducing development costs while allowing manufacturers to create vehicles with very different identities.


The original Renault Wind was a rare attempt to create a small roadster using everyday supermini engineering. Our imagined electric successor takes a similar approach, using the new Twingo as its starting point but giving the result a very different personality.

The two-seat cabin, short rear deck and pronounced rear haunches create a compact coupé shape, while the short sloping roof provides a visual link to the earlier car. At the front, rounded LED headlights and a slim grille bring the Wind into Renault's current design language, complemented by clean bodywork and distinctive electric alloy wheels.

We wouldn't expect a car like this to chase enormous performance figures. A modest increase over the standard Twingo's output, alongside carefully tuned suspension, could be enough to make it genuinely entertaining while keeping weight and costs under control.


A revived Wind should embrace colour. The Twingo has always worn its playful character openly, and a compact two-seat EV would look rather lost in a range limited to black, white and grey. Our four-car study shows how much the design changes with little more than paint.

For something designed to be fun rather than essential family transport, that matters. An electric Wind should be small enough to be sensible, but playful enough to make its owner smile.


Launched in 2010, the Renault Wind squeezed the idea of an open-top sports car into a body just 3.83 metres long. Sharing its foundations with the contemporary Twingo, it offered a 100hp 1.2-litre turbocharged petrol engine or a livelier 133hp 1.6-litre, both paired with manual gearboxes.

Its cleverest feature was a single-piece metal roof that rotated backwards in just 12 seconds, leaving the 270-litre boot space unaffected. British prices started at approximately £15,500, making it a relatively accessible little roadster.

The later Gordini edition added further visual character, but the Wind never achieved widespread popularity. Nevertheless, it brought something refreshingly different to the small-car market.


There is, of course, a commercial question: would enough people buy a two-seat electric Wind to justify bringing it back? The original demonstrated how limited that audience can be, and developing an entirely bespoke successor would be difficult to justify.

Sharing the Twingo's battery, motor and electronic systems could help change that equation, particularly if Renault resisted the temptation to make the car unnecessarily complicated.

An electric Wind wouldn't need to become the brand's next bestseller. It could offer something increasingly uncommon: an attainable little car bought for the pleasure of owning and driving it, rather than maximum practicality.

And Renault isn't alone in having a distinctive small car whose story might not be finished.


Nissan's new Pixo demonstrates how its long-standing partnership with Renault continues to deliver new models, with their collaboration now extending into Europe's smallest electric cars.

Revealed in September 2026, the compact EV shares much of its engineering with the new Twingo, including a 27.5kWh LFP battery and 82hp electric motor, offering up to 161 miles of WLTP range. Set to be produced by Renault in Slovenia, it gives Nissan an affordable entry point beneath the larger Micra EV.

Interestingly, TNY Design Studio published our own Nissan Pixo EV rendering on 13 September, ten days before Nissan revealed the production car's design.

Our exploration of this emerging small-EV family extends considerably further. Back in August, we imagined three possible directions for the next Dacia Spring, before Dacia officially unveiled its second-generation model in September.

We've also explored an affordable Alpine A190 electric hot hatch, and even a modern Mitsubishi i for Europe.

With the Pixo and Spring now revealed, these independent Design Studio explorations demonstrate just how much variety shared electric engineering could potentially support. And with Nissan bringing the Pixo name back, perhaps another distinctive little car from its past deserves consideration.


Where our Renault Wind EV takes a sportier approach, the Nissan Figaro embraces nostalgia. TNY Design Studio imagines the two cars as close mechanical relatives, sharing the Twingo's electric motor, battery and as much underlying engineering as practical. Producing them alongside one another could help make two distinctive, relatively low-volume models more financially viable.

Visually, however, the Figaro would be unmistakably different. Our rendering retains the original's charming proportions, rounded headlights and delicate chrome detailing, complemented by a contrasting cream metal roof. Pastel green bodywork, small amber indicators and cream-coloured wheels with polished hubcaps complete the retro appearance.

We've deliberately avoided oversized wheels, aggressive bumpers or unnecessary styling flourishes. The Figaro's appeal was always its individuality, and an electric successor should preserve that character.

Where the Pixo provides Nissan with practical, affordable electric transport, a revived Figaro could offer something rather more emotional: a small car people buy simply because they love it.


First shown at the 1989 Tokyo Motor Show, the Nissan Figaro arrived in 1991 as one of Nissan's imaginative Pike Factory creations. Beneath its 1950s-inspired bodywork were first-generation Micra mechanicals, including a turbocharged 987cc petrol engine producing 76PS, paired with a three-speed automatic gearbox.

Measuring just 3.74 metres long, the Figaro combined a folding fabric roof with cream leather upholstery, chrome detailing and four pastel colours inspired by the seasons. Production was limited to approximately 20,000 examples, with demand so strong that prospective buyers were selected by lottery.

Although originally sold exclusively in Japan, many subsequently found their way to Britain, where the Figaro developed an enthusiastic following.

More than three decades later, its enduring appeal demonstrates something rather important: a small car doesn't need impressive performance figures to become genuinely desirable.


The Renault Wind and Nissan Figaro might seem unlikely candidates for an electric revival, but both demonstrate how much character can be created from relatively ordinary small-car engineering.

Neither would be an obvious volume seller. A two-seat electric coupé and a retro-inspired Nissan would appeal to buyers looking for something beyond everyday practicality, and their commercial success would depend heavily on keeping development and production costs under control.

That is where the new Twingo's foundations become particularly interesting. Sharing batteries, motors and other components across several models could allow manufacturers to experiment with distinctive designs without developing entirely new cars from scratch.

Our imagined Wind and Figaro take two very different approaches to that opportunity: one playful and sporting, the other charming and nostalgic. Neither has been announced for production, but perhaps the next generation of affordable electric cars could offer more than sensible five-door hatchbacks.

After all, there should still be room for cars that make people smile.

These designs are unofficial and are not affiliated with or endorsed by Renault or Nissan. All manufacturer names, logos and trademarks remain the property of their respective owners.

items.title: Fast Estates Through the Ages – 16 Cars That Defined a Generation
items.summary: An estate car is supposed to be sensible. Room for the family, luggage, shopping and the occasional awkward trip to the tip. Yet for more than four decades, manufacturers have questioned why practicality should mean sacrificing performance. In 1981, Volvo transformed its famously boxy 245 into a turbocharged performance car. What followed…
items.content_html:
Volvo 245 Turbo

The Volvo 245 Turbo was introduced in 1981 and changed what an estate car could be. Volvo had already mastered practical family transport, but adding a turbocharger created the world's fastest estate car at the time.

Its 2.1-litre four-cylinder engine produced 155hp and 240Nm, driving the rear wheels through a four-speed manual gearbox with electric overdrive. Acceleration from 0–62mph took approximately nine seconds, with a top speed of 121mph — impressive figures for a boxy family car in the early 1980s.

Practicality remained exceptional. Volvo quoted 1,200 litres of luggage space, expanding to 2,150 litres with the rear seats folded, measured to roof height. The load floor stretched an impressive 1.88 metres.

American examples started at roughly $17,000 when new, equivalent to around £43,000 in today's money. European examples now typically command £7,000–£14,000, with restoration projects available for less.

Never officially sold in Britain, the 245 Turbo established a performance tradition Volvo would continue through the Volvo 740 Turbo, 850 T-5R and V70 R.


Ford Sierra 2.8i Ghia 4x4 Estate

When Ford introduced the Sierra in 1982, its rounded, aerodynamic bodywork looked revolutionary beside the boxy Cortina it replaced. Four years later, that distinctive design gained an unlikely performance derivative: the 2.8i Ghia 4x4 Estate.

Although it borrowed its mechanicals from the sporting XR4x4, Ford deliberately gave the estate more discreet Ghia badging. Its fuel-injected 2.8-litre V6 produced 150bhp, driving all four wheels through a five-speed manual gearbox and a rear-biased four-wheel-drive system.

Ford quoted 0–60mph in 9.2 seconds and a top speed of 124mph, respectable performance for a family estate in 1986.

The appeal extended beyond straight-line speed. Its aerodynamic styling, reassuring all-weather handling, self-levelling rear suspension and generous luggage compartment made it an unusually versatile performance car.

New examples started at approximately £14,000, equivalent to around £44,000 today. Survivors are now exceptionally rare, with recent UK auction results suggesting £6,000–£8,000 as a reasonable buying guide, depending on condition.

Understated, capable and distinctly British, the Sierra demonstrated that performance estates didn't need aggressive styling to be desirable.


Mercedes-Benz 300TE-24

By 1989, the fast estate was becoming something rather special. Mercedes-Benz demonstrated that practicality, luxury and impressive performance could coexist with the introduction of the 300TE-24, the flagship six-cylinder version of its W124 estate.

Underneath its understated styling sat a naturally aspirated 3.0-litre, 24-valve straight-six producing 220PS and 265Nm of torque. Power went to the rear wheels, with 0–62mph taking approximately 8.2 seconds and a top speed of 135mph.

Practicality remained exceptional. The enormous load area offered 530 litres of space, expanding to 1,770 litres with the rear seats folded. An optional rear-facing bench provided seating for seven, while self-levelling rear suspension helped maintain composure when heavily loaded.

Heavily optioned examples could approach £40,000 when new, equivalent to almost £100,000 today. Surviving cars can now be found for around £4,000–£9,000, although exceptional examples can exceed £12,000.

Just 6,282 examples were produced between 1989 and 1992, making the 300TE-24 a surprisingly rare machine and an important chapter in the development of the high-performance luxury estate. Photo: Dennis Elzinga / CC BY 2.0 (cropped).


BMW E34 M5 Touring

BMW's first proper M estate arrived in 1992, combining the E34 Touring's family-car practicality with the performance of its M5 saloon. Largely hand-finished at BMW Motorsport's Garching facility, it was a costly, low-volume proposition from the outset.

Its naturally aspirated 3.8-litre straight-six produced 340PS and 400Nm, driving the rear wheels through a five-speed manual gearbox. A six-speed arrived in 1994. Acceleration from 0–62mph took approximately 5.9 seconds, while top speed was electronically limited to 155mph — a remarkable leap in estate-car performance, bringing genuine sports-car pace to a practical family vehicle.

Practicality was equally impressive, with a 460-litre boot expanding to 1,450 litres, and separately opening rear glass making smaller items easier to load.

Originally priced at DM123,000 in Germany, approximately £45,000 at contemporary exchange rates, the M5 Touring would cost around £100,000 in today's money. Surviving examples now command roughly £35,000–£65,000, with exceptional cars fetching more.

Just 891 were produced between 1992 and 1995, all left-hand drive. Never officially sold in Britain, this exceptionally rare estate established a formula BMW's M division would return to in later generations.


Subaru Legacy GT Wagon

Subaru was building fast estates earlier than many enthusiasts realise. Its original turbocharged Legacy GT Wagon arrived in Japan in 1989 with 200PS, but the second generation, launched in 1993, pushed the formula considerably further.

Its 2.0-litre flat-four employed sequential twin turbochargers, producing 250PS and 309Nm. Permanent all-wheel drive and a choice of manual or automatic transmissions delivered serious performance, without sacrificing five-seat practicality or a generous load area.

Subaru even demonstrated the car's capabilities at Bonneville in September 1993, setting an officially recognised production-estate speed record of 249.981km/h (155mph).

The story continued with the smaller Impreza WRX Sport Wagon, offering 220PS in 1993, while the 1996 Legacy GT-B reached 280PS with its manual gearbox and introduced Bilstein suspension.

Originally priced from approximately ¥2.74 million in Japan, equivalent to around £16,000 at the time or £36,000 today, surviving twin-turbo Legacys can now cost roughly £3,000–£10,000 in Britain. Often overshadowed by Subaru's rallying achievements, the Legacy deserves recognition for helping establish the affordable, all-wheel-drive performance estate.


Audi RS2 Avant

By 1994, fast estates were already serious performance cars. Audi's contribution was the RS2 Avant, developed with Porsche and the first model to wear the now-familiar RS badge.

Its turbocharged 2.2-litre five-cylinder produced 315PS and 410Nm, delivered through a six-speed manual gearbox and quattro all-wheel drive. Acceleration from 0–62mph took 5.4 seconds, with a top speed of 163mph. Porsche helped develop the brakes and suspension, contributed its distinctive Cup alloy wheels and mirrors, and assembled the RS2 at Zuffenhausen.

Despite its performance, the RS2 remained a genuine family estate, seating five and offering 370 litres of boot space, expanding to 1,200 litres with the rear seats folded.

The UK launch price was £45,705, equivalent to roughly £100,000 today. Surviving examples now command approximately £40,000–£60,000, with exceptional cars fetching considerably more.

Just under 3,000 were produced between 1994 and 1995, including around 180 right-hand-drive examples for Britain. Its lasting significance was establishing Audi's RS lineage, bringing Porsche-influenced engineering to a practical, understated estate car.


Volvo 850 T-5R

Volvo had built fast estates before, but the 850 T-5R gave the concept a more extrovert personality. Launched in 1995, following the memorable appearance of the 850 estate in the 1994 British Touring Car Championship, its cream-yellow paint, deep front spoiler and graphite Titan wheels were impossible to miss.

Its turbocharged 2.3-litre five-cylinder produced 240bhp, aided by a short-duration overboost system. Power went to the front wheels through a five-speed manual or four-speed automatic gearbox. Volvo quoted 0–62mph in 7.0 seconds for the estate and an electronically limited 155mph top speed.

Practicality remained thoroughly Volvo. The square load area offered approximately 420 litres, growing to 1,580 litres with the rear seats folded. Five seats, side-impact protection and an integrated child booster made it a remarkably versatile family car.

The UK launch price was £28,840, equivalent to approximately £62,000 today. Surviving examples typically fetch £8,000–£18,000, although outstanding cream-yellow estates can command more.

Following the earlier 245 Turbo, the T-5R helped define a new generation of performance Volvos, paving the way for the 850 R and later V70 R.


Saab 9-5 Aero SportWagon

Saab's 9-5 Estate arrived in 1998, but the Aero followed in 1999, returning the Swedish manufacturer to the fast-estate market after a long absence. It approached performance in unmistakably Saab fashion: understated styling, impressive mid-range acceleration and turbocharged power rather than a large engine.

Its 2.3-litre turbocharged four-cylinder produced 230bhp, driving the front wheels through a five-speed manual or optional automatic gearbox. The manual estate managed 0–62mph in approximately 7.3 seconds and a top speed of 149mph. A 2001 facelift increased output to 250bhp, delivering stronger performance.

Practicality remained a priority, with 416 litres of boot space expanding to 1,490 litres. Clever floor-mounted cargo rails helped secure luggage, while an optional sliding load floor made loading particularly easy.

Around 2000, the Aero Estate cost approximately £29,000 new, equivalent to roughly £57,500 today. Used examples now typically cost £2,500–£6,000, although particularly well-preserved cars can exceed £8,000.

The Aero demonstrated that a fast estate could combine genuine performance with comfort, individuality and thoughtful Scandinavian engineering.


Mercedes-AMG E63 Estate

Mercedes-Benz had a long history of powerful estate cars, but the E63 AMG introduced in 2006 represented another significant development. Replacing the supercharged E55, it introduced an entirely new engine developed independently by AMG, rather than a modified Mercedes-Benz unit.

That hand-built, naturally aspirated 6.2-litre V8, badged as a 6.3, produced 507bhp and 630Nm of torque. A seven-speed automatic sent power to the rear wheels, delivering 0–62mph in just 4.6 seconds and an electronically limited top speed of 155mph.

Yet it retained the qualities that made the E-Class estate so appealing. Its enormous 690-litre boot expanded to 1,950 litres with the rear seats folded, while self-levelling air suspension helped maintain comfort even when heavily loaded.

British buyers paid approximately £68,000 new, equivalent to around £123,000 today. Surviving examples can now cost £13,000–£22,000, although maintaining the sophisticated suspension and high-performance V8 can make ownership considerably more expensive than the purchase price suggests.

BMW's 2007 M5 Touring offered a fascinating alternative, with a 507PS, 5.0-litre V10 and 0–62mph in 4.8 seconds, against the E63's 4.6. Both were remarkably quick, but the real choice was character — the Mercedes' deep, thunderous V8 or the BMW's distinctive, high-revving V10 soundtrack.


Chrysler 300C SRT8

The Chrysler 300C was already turning heads in Britain long before the SRT-8 arrived. Its imposing chrome grille, high waistline, enormous proportions and unmistakably American styling made it stand out amongst European executive cars. The Touring estate was arguably even more distinctive, combining that bold appearance with a vast, practical rear end.

But in 2007, the SRT-8 Touring took things considerably further, introducing a 6.1-litre HEMI V8 producing 425bhp and 569Nm of torque. Driving the rear wheels through a five-speed automatic, it could reach 60mph in approximately five seconds and continue to 168mph.

There was an interesting German connection, too. Developed during the DaimlerChrysler era, the 300C incorporated Mercedes-derived suspension engineering and other components related to the E-Class, although it wasn't simply a rebodied Mercedes. The estate was also closely related to America's Dodge Magnum.

At approximately £41,000 new, the SRT-8 Touring considerably undercut German performance estates, including the £67,000 BMW M5 Touring. Practicality remained impressive, with a 630-litre boot expanding to around 1,600 litres.

Today, genuine SRT-8 estates are particularly scarce in Britain, although examples occasionally appear around £10,000 - £12,000. It wasn't subtle, economical or particularly sophisticated, but few estates offered quite so much presence, power and character for the money.


Cadillac CTS-V Sport Wagon

Introduced in America in 2011, the Cadillac CTS-V Sport Wagon was one of the great performance estates Britain never officially received. Its sharp, angular bodywork, distinctive vertical rear lights and purposeful stance gave it an unmistakably American identity, yet it remains relatively unknown to British enthusiasts.

Underneath sat a supercharged 6.2-litre LSA V8 producing an extraordinary 556bhp and 747Nm of torque. Power reached the rear wheels through either a six-speed manual or automatic transmission, with Cadillac quoting 0–60mph in just 4.0 seconds.

The CTS-V offered considerably more than straight-line performance. Magnetic Ride Control suspension and Brembo brakes helped manage its enormous power, while the estate body provided 720 litres of luggage capacity, expanding to 1,642 litres with the rear seats folded, using American measurements.

American prices started at approximately $63,000, equivalent to around $93,000 today. Surviving examples now regularly command $50,000–$80,000, with desirable manual versions particularly sought after. British buyers face the additional challenge of sourcing and importing a left-hand-drive example.

With fewer than 1,800 produced between 2011 and 2014, the CTS-V Sport Wagon remains exceptionally rare. Its combination of supercharged V8 power, genuine practicality and an available manual gearbox makes it one of America's most remarkable performance estates.


Jaguar XFR-S Sportbrake

Jaguar had been producing powerful sporting saloons for decades, but it wasn't until 2014 that the British manufacturer introduced its first true high-performance estate. Based on the formidable XFR-S saloon, the Sportbrake combined elegant proportions with enlarged air intakes, 20-inch alloys and a prominent roof spoiler. Particularly in striking Ultra Blue, it was anything but discreet.

Underneath sat Jaguar's magnificent 5.0-litre supercharged V8, producing 542bhp and 680Nm of torque. An eight-speed automatic drove the rear wheels, delivering 0–60mph in 4.6 seconds and an electronically limited top speed of 186mph.

Despite its aggressive character, the Jaguar retained a practical 550-litre boot, expanding to 1,675 litres with the rear seats folded. Revised rear suspension, adaptive dampers and an electronic differential helped control its considerable performance.

British prices started at £82,495, equivalent to approximately £115,000 today. Recent auction sales have ranged from around £25,000 to £37,000, although exceptional examples could command considerably more.

The XFR-S Sportbrake was also extraordinarily rare, with reportedly just 61 examples produced worldwide. Its combination of British design, supercharged V8 power and genuine estate practicality makes it a fascinating, often overlooked chapter in Jaguar's history.


Volvo V60 Polestar

Another performance estate that attracted attention through more than speed and practicality was the Volvo V60 Polestar. Its striking Rebel Blue paint offered a refreshing splash of colour when so many performance cars appeared in greys, silvers and blacks.

Developed with Volvo's motorsport partner Polestar, its 3.0-litre turbocharged straight-six produced 350PS and 500Nm of torque. All-wheel drive and a six-speed automatic delivered 0–62mph in five seconds, with an electronically limited 155mph top speed.

The engineering extended to adjustable Öhlins dampers, substantially stiffer springs and powerful Brembo brakes. Practicality remained respectable, with 430 litres of luggage space beneath the window line, expanding to 1,241 litres with the rear seats folded.

Priced at £49,775 new, approximately £70,000 in today's money, the original V60 Polestar was also genuinely exclusive. Just 125 examples were allocated to the UK in 2014, each generously equipped.

Today, examples typically command around £23,000–£30,000. A later 2.0-litre four-cylinder version increased output to 367PS, but the original six-cylinder retains its own appeal. Interestingly, the original 3.0-litre straight-six also had a Welsh connection, having been manufactured at Ford's Bridgend engine plant.


Škoda Octavia vRS Estate

The fourth-generation Octavia vRS appeared in 2020, continuing Škoda's tradition of combining performance with everyday practicality. Sharper styling, lowered suspension and distinctive vRS detailing gave the spacious family estate a sporting character without sacrificing its versatility.

Initially, the 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol engine produced 245PS and 370Nm, driving the front wheels through a seven-speed DSG automatic. It reached 62mph in 6.7 seconds, while the 2024 facelift increased power to 265PS, reducing that time to 6.5 seconds.

Today, a new Octavia vRS Estate starts at £41,765, while early fourth-generation petrol examples can be found used from approximately £18,000. That makes it one of the more accessible modern performance estates.

Sharing Volkswagen Group engineering with the Golf R Estate and CUPRA Leon Sportstourer, the Škoda offers slightly better fuel efficiency. However, the contemporary 320PS Golf R Estate featured all-wheel drive and reached 62mph in just 4.9 seconds, making it 1.8 seconds quicker than the original Octavia.

Practicality remains the Škoda's strongest advantage, with 640 litres of luggage capacity expanding to 1,700 litres with the rear seats folded. That's more than the Golf R Estate's respective 611 and 1,642 litres.


Peugeot 508 PSE SW

Introduced to Britain in 2021, the Peugeot 508 Sport Engineered SW was a distinctive French alternative to the conventional performance estate. Its low roofline, wide stance, dramatic aerodynamic detailing and frameless door glass gave it remarkable road presence.

Inside, Peugeot's impressive i-Cockpit combined a compact steering wheel with digital instruments, sculpted controls and richly trimmed sports seats. It felt special even before the engine started.

A turbocharged 1.6-litre petrol engine worked alongside two electric motors, producing a combined 360PS and 520Nm. Four-wheel drive and an eight-speed automatic helped it reach 62mph in just 5.2 seconds, making it Peugeot's most powerful production car at launch.

Practicality remained impressive, with 530 litres of luggage space, expanding to 1,780 litres. The plug-in hybrid system also offered up to 26 miles of electric driving, making everyday journeys surprisingly economical when regularly charged.

Originally priced at £55,795 in Britain, the PSE was an expensive proposition. Today, used examples can be found from around £19,000, making this unusual, beautifully designed French performance estate considerably more accessible.


BMW M3 Touring

BMW had built its first M5 Touring 30 years earlier, but an M3 estate remained conspicuously absent. That changed in 2022, when the G81 M3 Touring made its debut at Goodwood, finally bringing the celebrated M3 formula to a practical five-door body.

Offered exclusively as a Competition xDrive, its twin-turbocharged 3.0-litre straight-six produced 510PS and 650Nm. An eight-speed automatic and all-wheel drive delivered 0–62mph in just 3.6 seconds, with a limited top speed of 155mph, or 174mph with the optional M Driver's Package.

A 2024 update subsequently increased output to 530PS, although the official 0–62mph time remained unchanged at 3.6 seconds. Despite its extraordinary performance, practicality remained intact. The 500-litre boot expanded to 1,510 litres, while the separately opening rear window made smaller items easier to load.

British prices started at £80,550, while early used examples can now be found from around £59,000, usually with higher mileages. Flared wheel arches, aggressive bumpers and four exhaust pipes ensured it looked every bit as serious as its performance suggested.

Four decades after the Volvo 245 Turbo, the M3 Touring demonstrated just how far the performance estate had evolved, while remaining faithful to the original idea.


From Volvo's pioneering turbocharged estates to Subaru's all-wheel-drive wagons, Saab's understated Aero and Jaguar's supercharged V8, the history of the fast estate has never belonged to one manufacturer or country. Chrysler and Cadillac contributed American muscle, while Peugeot demonstrated how hybrid technology could combine performance with efficiency.

Now electrification is taking the concept further. BMW's plug-in hybrid M5 Touring produces 727PS and reaches 62mph in 3.6 seconds, while Porsche's fully electric Taycan Turbo S Sport Turismo manages the same sprint in just 2.4 seconds.

And a new generation of Chinese manufacturers is joining the competition. Denza's Z9GT offers 0–62mph in just 2.7 seconds, while the Zeekr 7GT manages 3.3 seconds. Avatr's striking 06T estate promises even stronger acceleration at 2.78 seconds, with European sales planned for 2027.

More than four decades after the Volvo 245 Turbo, the technology may be changing, but the appeal remains remarkably familiar. Whether powered by a turbocharged four-cylinder, a thunderous V8, a plug-in hybrid or electricity alone, the best fast estates combine everyday practicality with the simple enjoyment of driving.

items.title: The Art of Thinking Small – Europe's M1E Revolution Explored
items.summary: At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Citroën’s reborn 2CV offered an intriguing glimpse of what Europe’s small-car market could look like from 2028. Compact, electric, full of character and targeting a price of around €15,000, it represents a return to the idea that affordable cars can still be desirable. Behind that vision…
items.content_html:
Citroën didn't stop at the passenger car. Alongside the 2CV, Paris brought the wonderfully boxy 2CV Fourgonnette Concept, a modern interpretation of the little delivery van that once served shopkeepers, farmers and tradespeople across Europe.

It offers an intriguing glimpse of how the affordable electric-car movement could eventually extend into commercial vehicles. A small, lightweight electric van with modest running costs could make enormous sense for local businesses.

There is one important distinction. The proposed M1E classification applies to passenger cars rather than commercial vehicles, and Citroën describes the Fourgonnette as a design study rather than a confirmed production model.

Nevertheless, the principle seems too sensible to overlook. If Europe can rediscover the affordable small car, perhaps the affordable little van could follow.


Our TNY rendering imagines how Citroën’s 2CV concept might evolve into a production-ready car for 2028. The original, unveiled in 1948, remained in production until 1990, with more than five million examples built across the 2CV family. Its appeal came from comfort, simplicity, practicality and a character rarely found in inexpensive cars.

Citroën has made affordable city cars work more recently. Built from 2005 to 2022, the C1 shared its development and Czech production line with the Peugeot 107/108 and Toyota Aygo, spreading costs across three brands. When it disappeared, Citroën was left with a sizeable gap between the Ami quadricycle and the larger C3.

At just 3.76 metres long, the new 2CV could fill that space. Citroën is targeting around €15,000, an ambitious figure when the ë-C3 starts at £18,495 in Britain after a £1,500 government grant, itself great value in the small car market. Making it affordable is one challenge; making it desirable is where the 2CV name could shine.


Few manufacturers understand the appeal of a small car quite like Fiat. The original 500 helped put post-war Italy on wheels, while the Panda of 1980 turned minimalism into something ingenious. The Cinquecento and Seicento carried that tradition into the 1990s, proving that affordable needn't mean forgettable.

Our TNY Koala imagines the next chapter: a friendly, compact electric Fiat taking inspiration from the Panda without simply recreating the past. It would give Fiat a useful step between the Topolino quadricycle and today's 500 and Grande Panda, combining proper small-car versatility with a genuinely compact footprint.

UK pricing makes the possibility especially interesting. The Topolino starts at £8,995, the electric 500e at £17,245 after a £3,750 government grant, and the Grande Panda Hybrid at £19,995.

If the future Koala arrived below £20,000, Fiat could offer four distinct entry-level models under that threshold — an increasingly unusual breadth of affordable small cars.


Our rear three-quarter rendering keeps the Koala's design pleasingly straightforward, with a practical tailgate and simple, distinctive lighting. It is the sort of car that could remain attractive without a complete redesign every few years.

While the styling and Koala name remain speculative, Fiat's forthcoming small EV is expected to share Stellantis's new E-Car architecture with the Citroën 2CV. Production of the first E-Car models is planned for Italy in 2028, allowing development costs to be spread across different brands.

That scale becomes particularly important under the proposed M1E framework. Eligible small electric cars built in the EU could count as 1.3 vehicles towards manufacturers' fleet CO₂ calculations until 2034. The European Commission also hopes to limit new regulatory requirements over a ten-year period.

Neither measure guarantees a low purchase price, and existing safety standards remain, but both could encourage longer production runs, modest facelifts and better-finished affordable cars.


Peugeot has an obvious opportunity within this emerging family of small electric cars. The original 108 disappeared in 2022, leaving the larger 208 as Peugeot's smallest conventional passenger car. Our TNY rendering imagines its return as a 4-metre electric supermini, combining Peugeot's latest design language with the affordable engineering developed for Citroën and Fiat.

But why stop at three brands? Stellantis has already confirmed that its E-Car programme is intended to support multiple manufacturers, spreading development costs across greater production volumes.

Peugeot could offer something sharper and sportier, while Opel and Vauxhall could develop their own interpretations for continental European and British customers. Each could share the same fundamental engineering while retaining a distinct appearance and personality.

Although additional models remain unconfirmed, the potential is considerable. With an expensive new platform already under development, expanding the family across Stellantis could make affordable electric cars considerably more viable.


If the 108 represents the return of the affordable city car, our Peugeot 1008 explores a different opportunity. Roughly four metres long, with an upright crossover stance and the assertive face of Peugeot's latest electric models, this TNY concept sits beneath the 2008 but aims to feel substantial, refined and desirable.

M1E is often discussed as a route to €15,000 EVs. Yet the proposed rules define the category by being fully electric and no longer than 4.2 metres; they set no price ceiling or power limit. What if Peugeot used the same shared Stellantis foundations to build something genuinely upmarket?

Our hypothetical brief imagines around 150hp, a 250-mile WLTP target and a price close to £27,000, with particular attention paid to ride comfort, sound insulation, interior materials and long-term durability. These are TNY ambitions, not confirmed specifications or capabilities of the E-Car platform.

The Commission's proposed ten-year period of regulatory stability could strengthen that business case, letting Peugeot invest in a carefully finished small car and keep it attractive through a long production life, with restrained facelifts and evolving technology. M1E needn't only make small cars cheaper; it could make them better.


Renault Group may have an even clearer opportunity to make M1E work. Its all-new Dacia Spring provides a compelling starting point: now built in Slovenia, measuring 3.85 metres long and priced from €17,900 in France before incentives.

Underneath sits Renault Group's cost-conscious RG-EV Small architecture, developed to deliver modern electric motoring without unnecessary expense.

Our TNY Sandero EV imagines that thinking applied to something more substantial. Taking inspiration from the new Spring's upright stance, protective cladding and crisp lighting, we've developed a five-door hatchback with the passenger space and luggage capacity expected of a Sandero. It would be a genuinely useful everyday car, rather than a purely urban runabout.

At around 4.1 metres, it would remain comfortably within M1E's proposed limit. Today's petrol Sandero starts at £14,765 in Britain, setting an understandably demanding benchmark for any electric successor.


From behind, our Sandero EV retains Dacia's practical priorities: an upright tailgate, robust bumper and useful proportions rather than a fashionable sloping roofline. Yet its greater size is also why it needn't be the cheapest Renault Group electric car.

The Spring and Twingo are compact four-seaters; a five-seat Sandero offering more boot space, potentially a larger battery and greater all-round versatility would naturally occupy a different position.

The real challenge is staying below the Renault 5 E-Tech, which currently starts at £21,495 in Britain after a £1,500 government grant. A Sandero EV needn't undercut the smaller Spring or Twingo to make sense. With shared LFP technology, simplified components and the prospect of M1E regulatory stability, Renault Group could produce a spacious, lower-cost alternative to the Renault 5.

European manufacturing could bring additional proposed CO₂ incentives, too, although neither a production Sandero EV nor its specification or price has been confirmed.


Dacia looks ideally placed to exploit M1E, but Renault itself has considerably less room for another small electric car. The new Twingo E-Tech provides an accessible entry point, with the Renault 5 and 4 already covering the ground above. Add an all-new Clio, arriving in Britain in 2027 with petrol and hybrid powertrains, and Renault's smaller-car range looks unusually complete, modern and competitively priced.

Even the refreshed Mégane E-Tech almost straddles the M1E boundary. At 4,199mm long, it sits just 1mm below the proposed 4.2-metre limit.

Its latest version starts at £28,245 in Britain after the £3,750 government Electric Car Grant, bringing a 67kWh LFP battery, 220hp, up to 306 miles of WLTP range and 165kW rapid charging. That's a remarkably strong package for the money, without needing another model squeezed into the range.

For now, the clearest Renault Group opportunity to broaden affordable electric motoring may therefore sit with Dacia.


Volkswagen revealed the ID.EVERY1 concept in March 2025, previewing a 3.88-metre electric car scheduled for production in 2027 and targeting around €20,000. Our TNY ID.Lupo rendering imagines how that concept might evolve into a production Volkswagen, reviving one of the brand's familiar small-car names.

Its timing could prove fortunate. M1E remains a proposal, but the intended 4.2-metre ceiling means the ID.EVERY1 is already the right size.

Volkswagen could engineer the car around the expected framework from day one, rather than face significant revisions later. Whether it receives the proposed benefits will depend on the final regulations and where the vehicle is manufactured.

The ID. Polo now starts at £22,445 in Britain after the £1,500 government grant. Yet Volkswagen still needs a smaller electric car capable of bringing its entry price closer to £15,000–£20,000, and the ID.Lupo could be vital to keeping the brand competitive.


Škoda has already demonstrated the value of sharing small-car engineering. Its original Citigo was closely related to the Volkswagen up! and SEAT Mii, while the electric Citigo-e iV arrived in 2019. Our TNY rendering imagines a modern successor, sharing its foundations with Volkswagen's forthcoming entry-level EV.

The Fabia and Scala demonstrate Škoda's ability to deliver generous space and practicality for modest money, while the new Epiq brings that philosophy to electric crossovers. However, with prices starting at £24,950, the Epiq retains a relatively high entry price in an increasingly competitive small-EV market. A smaller, more affordable Citigo EV could therefore fill an important gap, giving this value-conscious brand a genuinely accessible electric city car.

Volkswagen Group already shares development costs across the ID.Polo, ID.Cross, Cupra Raval and Škoda Epiq. Extending that approach to smaller models could make M1E particularly attractive.

From Stellantis to Renault Group and Volkswagen Group, Europe's established manufacturers have the brands, experience and industrial capacity to embrace this opportunity. But affordable electric motoring needn't remain exclusively European territory. Chinese manufacturers willing to establish production within the EU could also benefit, potentially bringing fresh competition to Europe's smallest-car market.


MG could become one of the most interesting beneficiaries of M1E. Its petrol and Hybrid+ MG3, alongside the electric MG4 and newer MG4 EV Urban, have helped establish the Chinese-owned British marque as a serious contender across Europe. Yet there remains an opportunity for something smaller and more affordable.

Our TNY MG GO, previously explored in Design Studio, imagines a practical five-door electric hatchback measuring approximately four metres long. With a target price below £20,000, it could give MG an appealing entry point into electric ownership, complementing its increasingly comprehensive small-car range.

Crucially, MG has announced a €200 million manufacturing facility in Galicia, Spain, with production scheduled for 2028 and capacity for 120,000 vehicles annually.

Under the proposed European rules, Chinese ownership would not necessarily prevent M1E eligibility. However, EU assembly alone would be insufficient: vehicles would also need to satisfy European component or battery-origin requirements.

Whether MG would manufacture such a small car in Spain remains speculative, but the opportunity is certainly there.


Chery is already thinking smaller. In April 2026, its head of engineering, Peter Matkin, confirmed development of a new architecture for cars measuring less than four metres, opening opportunities beyond the group's predominantly SUV-focused range.

TNY recently explored that possibility with our Jaecoo 2 rendering: a distinctive 3.9-metre hatchback, with an estimated £19,000 starting price. An electric version would comfortably satisfy M1E's proposed dimensional requirements, although the model and its specifications remain entirely speculative.

Chery also has a growing European manufacturing presence. Through its partnership with Spanish manufacturer EBRO, the company is expanding production at Nissan's former Barcelona factory. Pre-production Jaecoo 5 models are expected by December 2026, with series production targeted for early 2027.

There is no confirmed plan to manufacture a Jaecoo 2 in Spain. However, a small electric model built there, incorporating sufficient European-sourced components or batteries, could potentially qualify for M1E's proposed incentives.

For Chery, European manufacturing and a new small-car platform could prove an exceptionally useful combination.


Perhaps it is fitting to finish where we began. The original 2CV demonstrated that affordable motoring could be practical, comfortable and full of character. Nearly eight decades after its introduction, those qualities remain just as relevant.

M1E will not transform Europe's small-car market overnight. The regulations remain proposals, batteries are still expensive, and manufacturers must find ways to make European production commercially competitive.

Yet the possibilities are considerable. From a €15,000 Citroën to a more sophisticated Peugeot, an affordable Dacia or even a Chinese-designed car manufactured in Europe, there needn't be one formula for success.

Above all, greater regulatory stability could encourage manufacturers to invest properly in their smallest cars, creating designs worth keeping in production for years rather than constantly replacing them.

If M1E succeeds, its greatest achievement may not simply be making small cars cheaper. It could make them genuinely desirable again.

TNY Design Studio renderings are independent, speculative illustrations and do not represent confirmed manufacturer designs or production plans. All proposed specifications and prices are estimates unless otherwise stated. M1E legislation remains subject to approval and amendment.

items.title: From Bestseller to Beyond – TNY Design Studio Explores Jaecoo's Future
items.summary: Few new car brands have arrived in Britain with quite the impact of Jaecoo. Launched here in January 2025, the Chinese SUV marque had already put its Jaecoo 7 at the top of the UK sales chart twice by September 2026, recording 10,813 registrations in that month alone. Behind it stands Chery,…
items.content_html:
Jaecoo’s next move could be its smallest SUV yet. Reports suggest the Jaecoo 3 will measure around 4.2 metres long, putting it alongside rivals such as the Ford Puma and Renault 4.

The newcomer is reportedly being developed with European buyers in mind, with hybrid and fully electric versions both possible. A 2027 launch has been suggested, although Jaecoo has yet to confirm a date or release final specifications.

For TNY Design Studio, we’ve imagined how Jaecoo’s familiar styling might translate into a smaller SUV. Our rendering keeps the bold front grille and angular bodywork of the larger models, with compact proportions suited to British roads. It could become an interesting alternative in an increasingly competitive market.


The Jaecoo 5 offers a useful indication of where the smaller Jaecoo 3 might fit. Measuring 4,380mm long, it starts at £24,555 on the road, while the larger Jaecoo 7 measures 4,500mm and costs from £30,165 in petrol form.

Both share the upright, distinctly Range Rover-inspired styling that has helped Jaecoo attract attention in Britain, offering a premium appearance without premium-brand prices. At approximately 4.2 metres long, the forthcoming Jaecoo 3 would be 180mm shorter than the 5.

Based on the existing range, we estimate that an entry-level hybrid could start somewhere around £20,000–£22,000, with an electric version potentially costing more. That would place it among some fiercely competitive small SUVs, while retaining the design that has made its larger siblings so recognisable.


Jaecoo has proved that distinctive styling and competitive pricing can win over British buyers. Yet the small-SUV market is fiercely competitive, with established rivals offering plenty of choice. If the Jaecoo 3 is to follow the success of the 5 and 7, can it deliver enough to stand out?

At the opposite end of Jaecoo’s expanding range, something considerably larger could be on the horizon. The Jaecoo 8 has only recently arrived in Britain, bringing seven-seat practicality and a starting price of £45,500. Yet reports suggest an even more ambitious model is being prepared: the Jaecoo 9, a potential new flagship aimed at the luxury SUV market.

The likely foundation is Chery’s Fulwin T11, already available in China. Measuring 5,205mm long, it is 385mm longer than the Jaecoo 8, with six seats arranged in a 2+2+2 configuration. Its range-extender hybrid system uses electric motors alongside a 1.5-litre petrol engine that generates electricity.

A Jaecoo 9 would take the brand beyond the affordable premium SUVs that established its reputation, potentially challenging considerably more expensive machinery. However, its final British specification, pricing and arrival date remain unconfirmed.

For TNY Design Studio, we’ve explored how the imposing Fulwin T11 could be transformed into a Jaecoo flagship, retaining its luxurious proportions while introducing the brand’s familiar styling.


Pricing could become one of the Jaecoo 9’s biggest advantages. With the smaller Jaecoo 8 starting at £45,500, TNY estimates the 9 could cost approximately £55,000–£60,000 in Britain. That would comfortably undercut the fully electric Kia EV9, priced from around £66,000, and Volvo EX90, starting at £73,160.

Reports suggest the Jaecoo 9 is destined for Britain, although the manufacturer has yet to announce a confirmed European launch date, specification or price. Much will depend on whether Chery’s range-extender hybrid technology can be adapted for European regulations. If Jaecoo gets the pricing right, its largest SUV could attract considerable attention.


While the Jaecoo 9 could take the brand further into luxury territory, an equally important opportunity lies at the opposite end of the market. In April 2026, Chery’s head of engineering, Peter Matkin, revealed that the company had begun developing a new platform for vehicles measuring less than four metres long. The aim is to compete in a substantial part of the European market that Chery’s predominantly SUV-focused range has yet to reach.

Although the project is underway, no launch date, specifications or intended brands have been confirmed. There is currently no official Jaecoo 2, but the new platform raises an interesting possibility.

For TNY Design Studio, we’ve imagined a compact Jaecoo hatchback measuring approximately 3.9 metres, bringing the brand’s distinctive styling into Fiat Grande Panda and Renault 5 territory.

Together, a potential Jaecoo 2 and Jaecoo 9 would represent two very different ambitions: affordable urban motoring at one end and six-seat luxury at the other. Between them, the 3, 5, 7 and 8 could form a remarkably comprehensive SUV-led range.
